strengths: Unified and elegant framework that combines continuous trajectory prediction with discrete token-based future RGB and depth generation within a single multi-modal architecture (Show-o backbone).
Conceptual insight of using the world model's discrete token prediction entropy as an intrinsic novelty reward to capture out-of-distribution driving trajectories during RL post-training.
Strong empirical performance on NAVSIM v1 and v2 benchmarks, attaining competitive state-of-the-art results (93.7 PDMS with best-of-N and 88.8 EPDMS) using only single-view front-camera inputs.
Thorough ablation study demonstrating that auxiliary RGB and depth supervision significantly boosts baseline planning representation quality prior to RL (improving PDMS from 86.2 to 88.5).
weaknesses: Marginal gain from the proposed exploration bonus: Table 4 reveals that the PDMS reward alone accounts for the bulk of the RL improvement (from 88.50 to 90.19 PDMS), while adding the image prediction uncertainty reward only improves performance from 90.19 to 90.36 (+0.17 PDMS). Without multiple seeds or standard deviations reported, it is difficult to determine whether this gain is statistically significant.

Architectural ambiguity in trajectory conditioning: The paper states that during RL, candidate trajectories are sampled and the world model is conditioned on them to generate future images. However, the exact conditioning mechanism (i.e., how continuous trajectory coordinates from the MLP head are injected or tokenized into the transformer during future token generation) is insufficiently detailed in Section 3.
Missing metrics in benchmark evaluation: In Table 5 (nuScenes comparison), the collision rates under the UniAD evaluation protocol are left entirely blank ('- - - -') without explanation.

Computational overhead and rollout latency: For each GRPO step, sampling G=8 candidate rollouts and performing iterative masked token generation for both RGB and depth frames across multiple timesteps is computationally heavy. The paper lacks discussion of RL training throughput, GPU hours, and whether world modeling generation is bypassed during test-time inference.

strengths: Unified Multi-Task Paradigm: Integrating dense visual (RGB) and geometric (depth) prediction into an autoregressive VLA architecture provides richer supervisory signals than traditional sparse waypoint imitation.

Strong Benchmark Performance: The method achieves competitive results on NAVSIM v1 (93.7 PDMS with Best-of-N, 90.4 single) and NAVSIM v2 (88.8 EPDMS), outperforming several existing methods including multi-sensor baselines.

Sound Conceptual Framework: Formulating out-of-distribution novelty via codebook prediction entropy of a learned world model, combined with safety-gating (PDMS > δ) in GRPO, is an intuitive approach to guide exploration.
weaknesses: Marginal Empirical Impact of the Core Exploration Bonus: While the paper positions the uncertainty-based exploration bonus as a central contribution, Table 4 demonstrates that adding the image reward on top of the standard PDMS reward only yields an improvement of +0.17 PDMS (from 90.19 to 90.36). Without error bars or variance across multiple seeds, it is difficult to determine whether this gain is statistically significant.

Ambiguity in Action-Conditioned Image Generation: In Section 3.5, the authors state that the world model is conditioned on candidate trajectory tau_i to perform future image generation. However, in Sections 3.3 and 3.4 (as well as Equations 2 and 3), the image generation losses do not explicitly show conditioning on the continuous trajectory tau. The exact mechanism by which a continuous trajectory vector tau_i is injected into the Show-o transformer backbone during GRPO rollouts remains underspecified.

Horizon Mismatch in Dynamics Anticipation: According to Appendix A, the model predicts RGB and depth images only 0.5 seconds ahead, whereas planning is evaluated over a 4.0-second horizon. Predicting one frame at 0.5s is insufficient to capture long-term consequences of a 4-second driving maneuver, limiting the claim of using world modeling to anticipate trajectory consequences.

Incomplete Validation on nuScenes: The exploration-driven RL stage (Stage 2) is entirely omitted on nuScenes (Table 5), testing only the Stage 1 supervised model. Furthermore, on nuScenes, the Stage 1 model underperforms several prior methods (e.g., OpenDriveVLA and EMMA) in L2 displacement error across both ST-P3 and UniAD protocols.

Computational Overhead and Efficiency: Sampling G=8 rollouts per step and autoregressively/mask-predicting visual tokens for both RGB and depth at every RL step introduces notable computational overhead. The paper lacks runtime and training efficiency analysis.

strengths: Unified framework: The paper effectively integrates trajectory planning and dense future generation (RGB and depth maps) within a unified Vision-Language-Action (VLA) backbone based on Show-o, demonstrating that multi-modal generation objectives provide valuable dense representation learning for autonomous driving.

Strong benchmark results: The proposed method achieves competitive performance on NAVSIM v1 (PDMS 90.4 without ensemble, 93.7 with best-of-N) and NAVSIM v2 (EPDMS 88.8), showing strong trajectory compliance and low collision rates.

Intuitive motivation: Leveraging world model prediction uncertainty as an intrinsic novelty/exploration bonus gated by driving safety metrics (PDMS) is conceptually intuitive and thoughtfully motivated for offline RL post-training.
weaknesses: Marginal empirical impact of the proposed exploration reward: In Table 4, the Stage 1 baseline achieves 88.50 PDMS. Applying standard GRPO with PDMS reward brings it to 90.19 (+1.69). Adding the proposed image uncertainty exploration bonus only increases it further from 90.19 to 90.36 (+0.17). Given that the uncertainty-based exploration mechanism is the primary conceptual contribution highlighted in the paper, an absolute gain of less than 0.2 PDMS points casts doubt on whether the exploration bonus provides a substantial, meaningful benefit beyond standard task reward optimization.

Unclear action-conditioning mechanism during rollout and generation: In Section 3.5, the authors state that candidate trajectories $\tau_i$ are sampled and the world model is conditioned on $\tau_i$ to generate future image tokens and compute entropy. However, Equations (2) and (3) in Section 3.4 show the generation probability conditioned only on past images, language command, and ego status embeddings, without explicit inclusion of the continuous trajectory $\tau$. The text does not detail how continuous waypoints are injected back into the discrete autoregressive/omni-attention generation backbone during rollouts.

Lack of evaluation on out-of-distribution (OOD) / long-tail scenarios: A central motivation of the paper is to alleviate the brittleness of imitation learning when encountering novel or OOD situations. However, experiments are conducted primarily on standard NAVSIM navtest splits. There is no dedicated stress testing, perturbation analysis, or targeted long-tail benchmark to empirically validate whether the policy truly generalizes better in OOD settings.

Computational overhead and rollout efficiency: Generating both RGB and depth token predictions across a large codebook ($K=8192$) for $G=8$ sampled candidate trajectories per GRPO iteration introduces non-trivial computational and memory overhead. The paper lacks discussion or empirical measurements regarding training throughput, inference latency, and computational costs during Stage 2.
